findings.summary: Page 2 renders almost entirely empty — a single callout at the top and roughly 80% of the page is blank board.
findings.evidence: The only body content is the callout "Wrappers Must Not Lie / Ending a wrapper with echo done returns 0 even after the real command failed - CI, set -e and && all read that as success." ending at ~y=420 of a 1440px-tall page; everything from there to the bottom border is empty.
findings.fix: Populate page 2 with the remaining blocks for "Wrapper Scripts That Report False Success" (code sample, bullet sections, tables) as on the other pages, or drop the page if its content was merged elsewhere.

findings.summary: A complete `case` dispatch example with `;;` and `esac` is taught on page 3, seven pages before `case` syntax, glob patterns and branch terminators are actually introduced on page 10.
findings.evidence: Page 3: heading "Dispatch, Then Propagate" over `case $1 in` / `  start) up ;;` / `  stop) down ;;` / `  restart) down; up ;;` / `esac`, plus the bullet "A long `if/elif` chain on one value flattens into `case`" — while page 10 is where "Shape of a case", "Globs, Not Regex" and "Branch Terminators" first explain `;;`, `*)` and pattern matching.
findings.fix: Move the init-script `case` example and the `if/elif` → `case` bullet onto page 10 alongside the `case` syntax material, and keep page 3 to status propagation only (`deploy; rc=$?` … `exit "$rc"`), branching with a plain `if` instead.

findings.summary: The description of `set -o pipefail` names the wrong command's status — it returns the rightmost non-zero status, not the first failure.
findings.evidence: "Pipeline status = LAST command; `set -o pipefail` = first failure" — the Bash manual states: "If pipefail is enabled, the pipeline's return status is the value of the last (rightmost) command to exit with a non-zero status, or zero if all commands exit successfully." So `(exit 3) | (exit 5)` under pipefail yields 5, not 3.
findings.fix: Change to: "Pipeline status = LAST command; `set -o pipefail` = last (rightmost) command that failed, else 0."

findings.summary: The page closes with an arithmetic-evaluation code block whose inverted truth rule is not explained until page 6.
findings.evidence: Page 1, under the heading "Chaining and Negation": "`(( 0 )); echo $?   # 1  - false` / `(( 5 )); echo $?   # 0  - true` / `n=3; echo $(( n * 2 ))   # 6`" — while `(( ))` and its callout "Inverted Truth: A numeric result of `0` gives exit status `1` (false)" first appear on page 6. Pages 3 (`(( rc == 0 ))`) and 5 (`(( 10 > 9 ))   # true`) also pre-use it.
findings.fix: Delete that code block from page 1 (it also has nothing to do with the "Chaining and Negation" heading it sits under) and keep the 0-is-false demo on page 6 next to the "Inverted Truth" callout.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: This one-callout page depends entirely on the rule that a script's exit status is its last command's status, which is not stated until page 3.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "Ending a wrapper with `echo done` returns `0` even after the real command failed" — the supporting rule "A script's own status is its ==last command's== status" appears on page 3, together with the `rc=$?` / `exit "$rc"` fix the callout implies but never shows.
findings.fix: Merge this callout into page 3 immediately above the "Dispatch, Then Propagate" / `exit "$rc"` material, so the rule and its violation are on the same page.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: The page opens with `[ ]` numeric and string comparison operators before page 4 introduces `[ EXPR ]` syntax and the operator families.
findings.evidence: Page 3's first block: "`[ 10 -gt 9 ]   # true, numeric` / `[ 10 \> 9 ]    # FALSE: '1' sorts under '9'` / `[ "$s" = "$t" ] # string equality`" — `-gt`, `=` and the mandatory-spaces rule are only defined on page 4 ("Numeric: `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge`", "Spaces Are Syntax", "String and Number Tests").
findings.fix: Move this code block to page 4, placing it directly under the "String and Number Tests" table where `-gt` versus `=` is defined.

findings.summary: `set -e` is discussed in a sidebox and relied on by three later pages, but its behaviour is never defined anywhere in the handbook.
findings.evidence: Page 4 sidebox "set -e Blind Spots": "Suppressed inside `if`, `while`, `until` conditions / Suppressed after `&&`, `||` and `!` / That is why a failing test never kills the script" — no page states the syllabus point "`set -e` aborts on non-zero". Page 2 already says "CI, `set -e` and `&&` all read that as success", and page 6 has "(( i++ )) # status 1 kills a set -e script".
findings.fix: Add a defining bullet on page 1 (with `set -o pipefail`): "`set -e` aborts the script on any non-zero status", then let the page 4 sidebox list its blind spots.

findings.summary: A `while` polling loop is used as an example four pages before `while`/`until` is taught, and it is unrelated to the exit-code table it follows.
findings.evidence: Page 4, between the "Codes Worth Memorising" table and the set -e sidebox: "`while ! nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done` / `echo 'postgres is up'`" — the `while CMD; do ...; done` form, `until`, and the mandatory `sleep` are only introduced on page 8 ("Two Directions", "Retry and Poll").
findings.fix: Remove this block from page 4; the same polling idiom already appears correctly on page 8 in the "until CMD" card (`until nc -z db 5432`).

findings.summary: The page ends with three `case`-pattern bullets that have no antecedent on a `read`/subshell page and precede the chapter that defines those patterns.
findings.evidence: Page 9 final bullets: "A quoted pattern is literal: `\"*\"` means an asterisk / Otherwise patterns match the expanded word directly / `shopt -s extglob` adds `@(a|b) ?(x) *(x) +(x) !(x)`" — nothing on page 9 mentions patterns or a matched word; "Globs, Not Regex" and the `case` word are introduced on page 10.
findings.fix: Move these three bullets to page 10 under the "Globs, Not Regex" table, and end page 9 on the `mapfile`/file-descriptor sidebox.

findings.summary: The bottom ~40% of page 3 is blank after the deploy/rc code block.
findings.evidence: Last content is the code block ending with "exit \"$rc\"" / "}" and its note "capture $? before anything else runs" at ~y=870; the remaining area down to the border at ~y=1385 is empty, and the right column stops at ~y=615.
findings.fix: Balance the page by moving content up from page 4 or adding the missing right-column blocks so the layout fills like pages 1 and 4-10.

findings.summary: The `set -e` blind-spot bullet states suppression applies to the command *after* `&&`/`||`, which is the one case where `set -e` does still abort.
findings.evidence: "Suppressed after `&&`, `||` and `!`" — Bash suppresses errexit for every command in an `&&`/`||` list *except the command following the final `&&` or `||``; so `set -e; check && do_thing` does exit when `do_thing` fails.
findings.fix: Reword to: "Suppressed for every command in an `&&`/`||` list except the last one; suppressed by `!`."

findings.summary: The claim that `[ "$f" = *.txt ]` compares against the literal `*.txt` ignores pathname expansion, which the shell applies to the unquoted pattern before `test` ever runs.
findings.evidence: "`[ \"$f\" = *.txt ]` compares to the literal `*.txt`" — with one matching file in the cwd it becomes `[ "$f" = a.txt ]`; with two or more it becomes `[ "$f" = a.txt b.txt ]` and fails with "too many arguments".
findings.fix: Reword to: "`[ \"$f\" = *.txt ]` doesn't pattern-match — the shell globs `*.txt` against the cwd first, then `test` does a literal string compare (or errors with 'too many arguments')."

findings.summary: The unqualified rule "Left side: quoting never needed" sits directly under a table that includes `[ ]`, where omitting quotes is exactly the documented bug.
findings.evidence: Sidebox "Rules of Thumb" → "Left side: quoting never needed", placed immediately after the table row "`[ ]`","yes","no","POSIX `sh`"; page 4 states the opposite for `[ ]`: "`[ $x = y ]` with `x` empty becomes `[ = y ]`".
findings.fix: Qualify the bullet: "Inside `[[ ]]`: left side needs no quoting (`[ ]` still does)."

findings.summary: `${arr[*]}` is shown unquoted while being credited with the joining behaviour that only happens when it is quoted.
findings.evidence: "`${arr[*]}` joins everything into one word" — unquoted, `${arr[*]}` is joined with a space and then word-split and globbed, giving the same multiple words as unquoted `${arr[@]}`; only `"${arr[*]}"` produces a single word (joined on the first char of `IFS`).
findings.fix: Change to: "`\"${arr[*]}\"` joins everything into one word (separator = first char of `IFS`)".

findings.summary: The for-loop page opens with a leftover arithmetic callout before any for-loop material, giving the learner an unrelated topic first.
findings.evidence: Page 7, first block: callout "Guard Idiom — `if (( count > 0 )); then` reads better and is safer than `[ \"$count\" -gt 0 ]`", ahead of the page's own first heading "Word-List Form".
findings.fix: Move this callout to the end of page 6, which is the arithmetic page, so page 7 opens on "Word-List Form".

findings.summary: The stdin-stealing trap is taught in terms of `while read`, whose mechanics are not introduced until page 9, with no forward pointer.
findings.evidence: Page 8: "`while read` consumes stdin; body commands fight for it" and sidebox "Stdin Thieves: `ssh`, `ffmpeg` and `mysql` eat the loop's input / The loop then exits after one iteration" — `read`, EOF-termination and `done < file` are first explained on page 9 ("The read Builtin").
findings.fix: Add "(see next page)" to the `while read` bullet, or move the "Stdin Thieves" sidebox onto page 9 next to the `while IFS= read -r line` idiom.

findings.summary: The pushpin graphic of the "pipe forks the loop into a subshell" note is drawn on top of the end of a code line.
findings.evidence: Code line "echo $count    # 0 - lost!" has the pink pin icon overlapping its trailing "lost!".
findings.fix: Shift the sticky note/pin down or left so the pin clears the last code line's text.
